Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(\phi\) denote Euler’s totient function.

### 1. Forced structure of the sets

Taking \(i=j\) gives
\[
|A_i|=i.
\]
If \(a\mid b\), then
\[
|A_a\cap A_b|=\gcd(a,b)=a=|A_a|,
\]
so
\[
A_a\subseteq A_b.
\]

For any element \(x\), let \(r\) be the smallest positive integer such that \(x\in A_r\). We claim that \(x\in A_n\) if and only if \(r\mid n\).

- If \(r\mid n\), then \(A_r\subseteq A_n\), so \(x\in A_n\).
- If \(x\in A_n\) but \(r\nmid n\), let \(g=\gcd(r,n)\). Then \(g<r\), and since \(x\in A_r\cap A_n\), we have \(x\in A_g\), contradicting the minimality of \(r\).

Thus each element \(x\) belongs exactly to the sets \(A_n\) whose indices are multiples of some integer \(r\).

For each positive integer \(m\), let
\[
B_m=\{x: x\in A_m \text{ and } x\notin A_k \text{ for all proper divisors } k\mid m\}.
\]
Then the sets \(B_m\) are disjoint, and
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{m\mid n}B_m.
\]
Hence
\[
|A_n|=\sum_{m\mid n}|B_m|=n.
\]
By induction using the standard identity \(\sum_{m\mid n}\phi(m)=n\), we get
\[
|B_m|=\phi(m).
\]

So each \(B_m\) contains exactly \(\phi(m)\) elements, and \(A_n\) is the union of the blocks \(B_m\) for \(m\mid n\).

---

### 2. Lower bound for the divisors of \(250\)

The positive divisors of \(250=2\cdot 5^3\) are
\[
D=\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250\}.
\]
For \(d\in D\), let
\[
M_d=\max A_d.
\]
Sort these eight numbers:
\[
N_1\le N_2\le \cdots \le N_8.
\]

For each \(c=1,\dots,8\), let
\[
T_c=\{d\in D: M_d\le N_c\}.
\]
Then \(|T_c|\ge c\). Also, \(T_c\) is divisor-closed: if \(d\in T_c\) and \(e\mid d\), then \(A_e\subseteq A_d\), so
\[
M_e\le M_d\le N_c,
\]
hence \(e\in T_c\).

The union
\[
U_c=\bigcup_{d\in T_c}A_d
\]
equals
\[
\bigcup_{m\in T_c}B_m,
\]
so
\[
|U_c|=\sum_{m\in T_c}\phi(m).
\]
Since every element of \(U_c\) is a positive integer at most \(N_c\), we have
\[
|U_c|\le N_c.
\]
Thus
\[
N_c\ge \sum_{m\in T_c}\phi(m).
\]

Now compute the smallest possible value of \(\sum_{m\in T}\phi(m)\) over divisor-closed \(T\subseteq D\) with at least \(c\) elements. The \(\phi\)-values of the eight divisors are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
\phi(d) & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 20 & 20 & 100 & 100
\end{array}
\]

The first \(c\) divisors in the order
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250
\]
always form a divisor-closed set. Therefore the minimum possible sum is just the prefix sum of the smallest \(c\) values:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
c & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8\\
\hline
\text{minimum} & 1 & 2 & 6 & 10 & 30 & 50 & 150 & 250
\end{array}
\]

Hence
\[
N_c\ge
\begin{cases}
1, & c=1,\\
2, & c=2,\\
6, & c=3,\\
10, & c=4,\\
30, & c=5,\\
50, & c=6,\\
150, & c=7,\\
250, & c=8.
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d=\sum_{c=1}^8 N_c
\ge 1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

---

### 3. Construction attaining the bound

We now construct the sets.

Choose disjoint sets \(B_m\) of size \(\phi(m)\) as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For all other positive integers \(m\), assign \(B_m\) any \(\phi(m)\) distinct positive integers larger than \(250\).

Define
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{m\mid n}B_m.
\]

For any \(i,j\),
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|
=\left|\bigcup_{m\mid i}\bigcap_{m\mid j}B_m\right|
=\sum_{m\mid \gcd(i,j)}\phi(m)
=\gcd(i,j),
\]
so the required condition is satisfied.

Now compute the maxima for the divisors of \(250\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max A_1 &= 1,\\
\max A_2 &= 2,\\
\max A_5 &= 6,\\
\max A_{10} &= 10,\\
\max A_{25} &= 30,\\
\max A_{50} &= 50,\\
\max A_{125} &= 150,\\
\max A_{250} &= 250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
=1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

The minimum possible value is therefore

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
